disclaimer: Study aid only, not legal advice and not affiliated with USCIS. Fees, timings and rules change. Check uscis.gov before you rely on anything here.

timeline.summary: Most people are sworn in 6 to 12 months after filing.
timeline.note: The national median from filing to decision has been around 5 to 6 months, but USCIS measures itself at the 80th percentile, where field offices range from roughly 3 to 17 months. Your field office is the single biggest factor, so look yours up rather than trusting a national number.

steps.title: Check that you qualify
steps.timingDetail: You can file up to 90 days early
steps.summary: Most applicants qualify on the 5-year rule; 3 years if you are married to and living with a U.S. citizen.
details: Be 18 or older and a permanent resident (green card holder) for 5 years — or 3 years if you have been married to and living with the same U.S. citizen for those 3 years.
Continuous residence: no single trip abroad of 6 months or more, and no trip of a year or more, during the qualifying period.
Physical presence: at least 30 months inside the U.S. out of the last 5 years (18 of 36 on the 3-year rule).
Have lived at least 3 months in the state or USCIS district where you file.
Good moral character over the qualifying period, and attachment to the Constitution.
Pass the English and civics tests, unless an exemption applies to you.
You may file up to 90 days before you hit the 5- or 3-year mark. Filing even a day earlier than that gets the application rejected.

steps.title: File Form N-400
steps.timingDetail: The clock starts the day USCIS receives it
steps.summary: Apply online with a USCIS account, or by mail. Online is $50 cheaper and easier to track.
details: Online filing at my.uscis.gov walks you through the form, lets you upload evidence, and shows case status and messages in one place.
Paper filing is required if you are requesting a reduced fee or a fee waiver.
Answer every question honestly. A wrong answer that looks like concealment is far more damaging than the fact you were hiding.
Keep a copy of everything you send, plus your receipt number.

steps.title: Receipt notice
steps.summary: USCIS confirms it has your application and gives you a receipt number.
details: The receipt number is how you track your case online and how you look up processing times for your field office.
Check that your name, date of birth and A-number are printed correctly. Errors here follow you through the whole case.
Filing also extends your green card while the case is pending — the receipt notice is the proof of that.

steps.title: Biometrics appointment
steps.summary: Fingerprints, photo and signature, for the FBI background check.
details: The appointment notice tells you the date, time and application support center. Reschedule before the date if you cannot make it — missing it without notice can get your case closed.
Bring the appointment notice and your green card.
USCIS often reuses fingerprints it already has and waives the appointment entirely. If that happens you get a notice saying so; it is not a problem.
The background check runs in the background from here on, and is a common reason a case sits quietly for a while.

steps.title: Interview and tests
steps.summary: An officer goes through your N-400 under oath, then gives you the English and civics tests.
details: Bring the appointment notice, your green card, your state ID, and every passport and travel document covering the qualifying period.
Bring originals of anything you only sent copies of, plus updates: new trips, a new address, a new job, anything that changed since you filed.
The officer confirms your answers on the N-400 out loud. This doubles as the speaking part of the English test.
Then the reading and writing tests, then the civics test.
You leave with Form N-652, which tells you what happened.

steps.title: Decision
steps.summary: Granted, continued, or denied — you normally find out before you leave.
details: Granted: your case moves to an oath ceremony.
Continued: something is missing, or you did not pass part of a test. For a failed test, USCIS schedules a second interview 60 to 90 days later and re-tests only the part you failed.
Denied: you can request a hearing with Form N-336 within 30 days of the denial, and you can reapply later.
Failing the same part twice means denial, so treat the second interview as the last one.

steps.title: Oath of Allegiance
steps.timing: Same day, or 2 weeks–3 months later
steps.timingDetail: Form N-445 is the ceremony notice
steps.summary: You become a citizen the moment you take the oath — not before.
details: Some field offices swear you in the same day as the interview. Otherwise Form N-445 arrives by mail, usually 2 to 3 weeks after the interview, with the date and place.
Complete the questionnaire on the back of the N-445 before you arrive: it asks what you have done since the interview (travel, arrests, marriage).
Bring your green card. You hand it in at the ceremony.
You take the Oath of Allegiance and receive your Certificate of Naturalization. Check every detail on it before you leave the building.

afterOath: Apply for a U.S. passport — it is the easiest proof of citizenship to carry, and it means you are not risking your only certificate.
Update Social Security so your record shows citizenship.
Register to vote. Many ceremonies have registration desks on site.
Keep the Certificate of Naturalization somewhere safe. Replacing it costs money and takes months.

methods.name: Online
methods.summary: Create a free account at my.uscis.gov, fill in the N-400, upload your evidence, and pay by card or bank transfer.
points: Case status, notices and secure messages all in one account.
Evidence is uploaded, so nothing gets lost in the mail.
Not available if you are requesting a reduced fee or a fee waiver.

methods.name: By mail
methods.summary: Download the current N-400 from uscis.gov/n-400, fill it in, and mail it with your evidence and payment to the address for your state.
points: Required if you want the reduced fee (Form I-942) or a fee waiver (Form I-912).
USCIS no longer takes personal checks for most paper filings — pay by card with Form G-1450, or by bank transfer with Form G-1650.
Use the edition of the form currently listed on uscis.gov. An out-of-date edition gets rejected.
Mail it so you get delivery confirmation.

checklist: A copy of both sides of your green card.
Every trip outside the U.S. of 24 hours or more in the last 5 years (3 on the marriage rule), with exact dates.
Tax records, or proof you have filed and are on a payment plan if you owe.
Marriage certificate and proof of your spouse's citizenship, if you are applying on the 3-year rule, plus divorce or death records ending any earlier marriage.
Court dispositions for any arrest, citation or conviction — including ones dismissed, expunged or sealed.
Your Selective Service number, if you are male and lived in the U.S. between the ages of 18 and 26.
Two passport-style photos, only if you live outside the U.S.

items.label: Biometric services
items.note: The separate $85 biometrics fee was folded into the filing fee on 1 April 2024.

items.label: Reduced fee (Form I-942)
items.note: Household income between 150% and 400% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines. Paper filing only.

items.label: Fee waiver (Form I-912)
items.note: Income under 150% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines, a means-tested benefit, or financial hardship. Paper filing only.

notes: The fee is not refunded if your application is denied or you withdraw it.
A lawyer is optional and is the largest variable cost if you use one. Accredited non-profits often help for free — find one through the DOJ recognised provider list.
If you claim a medical disability exception with Form N-648, the doctor's appointment is your cost.
After the oath, a U.S. passport is a separate State Department fee.

proposedChange.summary: DHS proposed on 23 June 2026 to raise the N-400 fee to $1,280 online and $1,330 by mail, and to end both the reduced fee and the fee waiver for naturalization. The comment period closed on 24 August 2026.
proposedChange.impact: Nothing changes until a final rule is published and takes effect. The fees above are the ones being charged now. If you are close to eligible and the cost matters to you, this is a reason to file sooner rather than later.

english.summary: Three parts, all judged by the officer at your interview.
parts: Speaking: assessed from how you answer the officer's questions about your N-400. There is no separate speaking test.
Reading: read 1 of up to 3 sentences correctly, out loud.
Writing: write 1 of up to 3 sentences correctly, as the officer dictates it.

civics.summary: Which set you get depends on the day USCIS received your N-400, not on when your interview is.

variants.label: Filed before 20 October 2025
variants.detail: The 2008 test: 10 questions drawn from 100, pass with 6.

variants.label: Filed on or after 20 October 2025
variants.detail: The 2025 test: 20 questions drawn from 128, pass with 12.

civics.note: The officer stops as soon as you have enough right answers, so a perfect start ends the test early.

exemptions.detail: 50 or older with 20 years as a permanent resident: no English test. Take the civics test in your own language with an interpreter.
55 or older with 15 years as a permanent resident: same as 50/20.
65 or older with 20 years as a permanent resident: no English test, and you only study the 20 specially marked civics questions. You are asked up to 10 of them and pass with 6.

exemptions.label: Medical exception (Form N-648)
exemptions.detail: A licensed doctor certifies a physical or developmental disability or mental impairment that prevents you from learning English, civics, or both. File it with your N-400 where you can.

tests.retake: Fail a part and USCIS re-tests only that part at a second interview, 60 to 90 days later. Failing the same part twice means the application is denied.
